A.explanation: This would depend on the size of the wire, but $n$ in $I = Anvq$ is a property of the material, not of the particular piece of wire.

B.explanation: Multiplying a count by volume does not give the concentration needed in $I = Anvq$ and has the wrong units for $n$.

C.explanation: Number per unit length ignores the cross-sectional area $A$, whereas the derivation counts carriers in a volume $A \times v\Delta t$.

D.explanation: In $I = Anvq$, $n$ is the number density of free charge carriers with unit $\text{m}^{-3}$.

hints: Look at the other symbols in $I = Anvq$: $A$ is the cross-sectional area in $\text{m}^2$ and $v$ is the drift speed in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
For $I$ to come out in amperes, $n$ must supply $\text{m}^{-3}$ so that $Anv$ gives carriers passing per second.
Ask whether $n$ describes the whole wire or the material itself: a longer wire has more total carriers but the same $n$.
walkthrough: Identify the equation: $I = Anvq$, where $A$ is cross-sectional area, $v$ is mean drift speed and $q$ is charge per carrier.
Picture carriers in a length $v\Delta t$ moving past a point in time $\Delta t$: the swept volume is $A v \Delta t$.
The number of carriers in that volume is (carriers per unit volume) $\times A v \Delta t$, so charge passed is $nAv\Delta t \times q$.
Since $I = Q/\Delta t$, this gives $I = Anvq$ only if $n$ is number per unit volume, with unit $\text{m}^{-3}$.
Options A and B use total number or number times volume, which would change with wire length, and option C omits area dependence. This is option D.
